text: GlideAjax calls are asynchronous - the callback that carries the server's answer runs later, not at the moment you call it. That timing is harmless in an onLoad script. It's a real trap inside onSubmit, because onSubmit has to return a value right now, and it can't pause and wait for the server.

Here's the broken version of that trap. The script calls GlideAjax, sets up a callback that will eventually set isBlocked, and then immediately returns the opposite of isBlocked. But the callback hasn't run yet - the server hasn't even responded. isBlocked is still its original false, every single time, so this script always lets the save through, silently defeating its own validation.

The real fix isn't to make GlideAjax wait - it's to stop trying to return a result you don't have yet. This version checks a passed-flag first; if it's not set, it fires the GlideAjax call and immediately returns false, blocking only this submit attempt while the real check runs in the background.

The actual decision happens inside the callback, once the server has responded. If the date is frozen, an error message appears and the form stays open. If it's clear, the script marks the check as passed and calls g_form.submit() itself - which re-runs onSubmit, and this time the guard at the top sees the passed flag and returns true, letting the save complete.

ServiceNow does ship an older synchronous method, getXMLWait, that genuinely blocks and waits for the response - and it's deprecated and discouraged for a real reason. While it waits, it freezes the entire browser tab's UI thread, so the user's screen becomes unresponsive for however long that round trip takes. The callback pattern is slower to write but never freezes the browser.

You now know why async GlideAjax breaks a naive onSubmit return, and the real pattern that fixes it: block first, decide in the callback, submit programmatically when valid.
